entries.1ebad2f0ce03455ef73cf15e78ae756e053bc8ed:
5 Lest perhaps the tempter has tempted you. By this term he teaches us that temptations are always to be dreaded, because it is the proper office of Satan to tempt. As, however, he never ceases to place ambushes for us on all sides, and to lay snares for us all around, so we must be on our watch, eagerly taking heed. And now he says openly what in the outset he had avoided saying, as being too harsh — that he had felt concerned lest his labors should be vain, if, peradventure, Satan should prevail. And this he does that they may be carefully upon their watch, and may stir themselves up the more vigorously to resistance.
1 Thessalonians 3:6-10
6. But now when Timotheus came from you unto us, and brought us good tidings of your faith and charity, and that ye have good remembrance of us always, desiring greatly to see us, as we also to see you:
6. Nuper autem quum venisset Timotheus ad nos a vobis, et annuntiasset nobis fidem et dilectionem vestram, et quod bonam nostri memoriam habetis semper, desiderantes nos videre, quemadmodum et nos ipsi vos:
7. Therefore, brethren, we were comforted over you in all our affliction and distress by your faith:
7. Inde consolationem percepimus fratres de vobis, in omni tribulatione et necessitate nostra per vestram fidem:
8. For now we live, if ye stand fast in the Lord.
8. Quia nunc vivimus, si vos stasis in Domino.
9. For what thanks can we render to God again for you, for all the joy wherewith we joy for your sakes before our God;
9. Quam enim gratiarum actionem possumus Deo reddere de vobis, in omni gaudio quod gaudemus propter vos coram Deo nostro;
10. Night and day praying exceedingly that we might see your face, and might perfect that which is lacking in your faith?
10. Nocte ac die supra modum precantes, ut videamus faciem vestram, et suppleamus quae fidei vestrae desunt?
entries.99fa6193c6e8ca266fa6c48230c2813210a57b52: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Thess.3.6" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Thess.3.6" sID="gen128155" type="section"/> <div sID="gen128156" type="x-p"/>He shews here, by another argument, by what an extraordinary affection he was actuated towards them, inasmuch as he was transported almost out of his senses by the joyful intelligence of their being in a prosperous condition. For we must take notice of the circumstances which he relates. He was in <hi type="italic">affliction</hi> and <hi type="italic">necessity:</hi> there might have seemed, therefore, no room for cheerfulness. But when he hears what was much desired by him respecting the Thessalonians, as though all feeling of his distresses had been extinguished, he is carried forward to joy and congratulation. At the same time he proceeds, by degrees, in expressing the greatness of his joy, for he says, in the <hi type="italic">first</hi> place, <hi type="italic">we received consolation:</hi> afterwards he speaks of a joy that was plentifully poured forth. <note n="557"> <div sID="gen128157" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ample et abondante</foreign>;” — “Large and overflowing.”<div eID="gen128157" type="x-p"/> </note> This congratulation, <note n="558"> <div sID="gen128158" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ceste façon de tesmoigner la ioye qu’il sent de la fermete des Thessaloniciens</foreign>;” — “This manner of testifying the joy which he feels in the steadfastness of the Thessalonians.”<div eID="gen128158" type="x-p"/> </note> however, has the force of an exhortation; and Paul’s intention was to stir up the Thessalonians to perseverance. And, assuredly, this must have been a most powerful excitement, when they learned that the holy Apostle felt so great consolation and joy from the advancement of their piety.<div eID="gen128156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen128159" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">6</hi> <hi type="italic">Faith and love</hi>. This form of expression should be the more carefully observed by us in proportion to the frequency with which it is made use of by Paul, for in these two words he comprehends briefly the entire sum of true piety. Hence all that aim at this twofold mark during their whole life are beyond all risk of erring: all others, however much they may torture themselves, wander miserably. The third thing that he adds as to their <hi type="italic">good remembrance </hi>of him, refers to respect entertained for the Gospel. For it was on no other account that they held Paul in such affection and esteem.<div eID="gen128159" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Thess.3.6" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen128155" osisID="1Thess.3.6" type="section"/>
entries.a9b742e7a7a916e15651018db31eab0569e48753: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Thess.3.8" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Thess.3.8" sID="gen128160" type="section"/> <div sID="gen128161" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">8</hi> <hi type="italic">For now we live</hi>. Here it appears still more clearly that Paul almost forgot himself for the sake of the Thessalonians, or, at least, making regard for himself a mere secondary consideration, devoted his first and chief thoughts to them. At the same time he did not do that so much from affection to men as from a desire for the Lord’s glory. For zeal for God and Christ glowed in his holy breast to such a degree that it in a manner swallowed up all other anxieties. “<hi type="italic">We live</hi>,” says he, that is, “we are in good health, <hi type="italic">if you persevere in the Lord</hi>.” And under the adverb <hi type="italic">now</hi>, he repeats what he had formerly stated, that he had been greatly pressed down by <hi type="italic">affliction</hi> and <hi type="italic">necessity;</hi> yet he declares that whatever evil he endures in his own person does not hinder his joy. “Though in myself I am dead, yet in your welfare I <hi type="italic">live</hi>.” By this all pastors are admonished what sort of connection ought to subsist between them and the Church — that they reckon themselves happy when it goes well with the Church, although they should be in other respects encompassed with many miseries, and, on the other hand, that they pine away with grief and sorrow if they see the building which they have constructed in a state of decay, although matters otherwise should be joyful and prosperous.<div eID="gen128161" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Thess.3.8" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen128160" osisID="1Thess.3.8" type="section"/>
entries.f08451a8e20c9ba3cd0157a31f193b319f1398a2: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Thess.3.9" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Thess.3.9" sID="gen128162" type="section"/> <div sID="gen128163" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">9</hi> <hi type="italic">For what thanksgiving</hi>. Not satisfied with a simple affirmation, he intimates how extraordinary is the greatness of his joy, by asking himself <hi type="italic">what thanks he can render to God;</hi> for by speaking thus he declares that he cannot find an expression of gratitude that can come up to the measure of his joy. He says that he rejoices <hi type="italic">before God</hi>, that is, truly and without any pretense.<div eID="gen128163" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Thess.3.9" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen128162" osisID="1Thess.3.9" type="section"/>
entries.741a862c3eba78568272e61400c4555d34f9dd7c:
10 Praying beyond measure. He returns to an expression of his desire. For it is never allowable for us to congratulate men, while they live in this world, in such unqualified terms as not always to desire something better for them. For they are as yet in the way: they may fall back, or go astray, or even go back. Hence Paul is desirous to have opportunity given him of supplying what is wanting in the faith of the Thessalonians, or, which is the same thing, completing in all its parts their faith, which was as yet imperfect. Yet this is the faith which he had previously extolled marvelously. But from this we infer, that those who far surpass others are still far distant from the goal. Hence, whatever progress we may have made, let us always keep in view our deficiencies, (ὑστερήματα,)
“Τστερήματα πίστεως. —Afterings of faith, as it may be significantly enough rendered, let but the novelty of the expression be pardoned.” —Howe’s Works, (London, 1822,) volume 3 page 70.—Ed
that we may not be reluctant to aim at something farther.
From this also it appears how necessary it is for us to give careful attention to doctrine, for teachers
“Les Docteurs et ceux qui ont charge d’enseigner en l’Eglise;” — “Teachers and those that have the task of instructing in the Church.”
were not appointed merely with the view of leading men, in the course of a single day or month, to the faith of Christ, but for the purpose of perfecting the faith which has been begun. But as to Paul’s claiming for himself what he elsewhere declares belongs peculiarly to the Holy Spirit, (1 Corinthians 14:14) this must be restricted to the ministry. Now, as the ministry of a man is inferior to the efficacy of the Spirit, and to use the common expression, is subordinate to it, nothing is detracted from it. When he says that he prayed night and day beyond all ordinary measure,
“Night and day praying exceedingly—Supplicating God at all times; mingling this with all my prayers; ὑπὲρ ἐχπερισσοῦ δεόμενοι, abounding and superabounding in my entreaties to God, to permit me to revisit you.” —Dr. A. Clarke.—Ed
we may gather from these words how assiduous he was in praying to God, and with what ardor and earnestness he discharged that duty.
1 Thessalonians 3:11-13
11. Now God himself and our Father, and our Lord Jesus Christ, direct our way unto you.
11. Ipse autem Deus et Pater noster, et Dominus noster Iesus Christus viam nostram ad vos dirigat.
12. And the Lord make you to increase and abound in love one toward another, and toward all men, even as we do toward you:
12. Vos autem Dominus impleat et abundare faciat caritate mutua inter vos et erga omnes: quemadmodum et nos ipsi affecti sumus erga vos:
13. To the end he may stablish your hearts unblameable in holiness before God, even our Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ with all his saints.
13. Ut confirmet corda vestra irreprehensibilia, in sanctitate coram Deo et Patre nostro, in adventu Domini nostri Iesu Christi, cum omnibus sanctis eius.
entries.1c2fa42bf7f9ce5a124b71deaff31ebadbee192b: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Thess.3.11" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Thess.3.11" sID="gen128179" type="section"/> <div sID="gen128180" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">11</hi> <hi type="italic">Now God himself</hi>. He now prays that the Lord, having removed Satan’s obstructions, may open a door for himself, and be, as it were, the leader and director of his way to the Thessalonians. By this he intimates, that we cannot move a step with success, <note n="562"> <div sID="gen128181" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Nous ne pouuons d’vn costé ne d’autre faire vn pas qui proufite et viene a bien</foreign>;” — “We cannot on one side or another take a step that may be profitable or prosperous.”<div eID="gen128181" type="x-p"/> </note> otherwise than under God’s guidance, but that when he holds out his hand, it is to no purpose that Satan employs every effort to change the direction of our course. We must take notice that he assigns the same office to God and to Christ, as, unquestionably, the Father confers no blessing upon us except through Christ’s hand. When, however, he thus speaks of both in the same terms, he teaches that Christ has divinity and power in common with the Father.<div eID="gen128180" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Thess.3.11" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen128179" osisID="1Thess.3.11" type="section"/>
entries.a3d99350438ceb61e4f554b37b90cb1d367cf6d0: <div annotateRef="Bible:1Thess.3.12" annotateType="commentary" osisID="1Thess.3.12" sID="gen128182" type="section"/> <div sID="gen128183" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">12</hi> <hi type="italic">And the Lord fill you</hi>. Here we have another prayer — that in the mean time, while his way is obstructed, the Lord, during his absence, may confirm the Thessalonians in holiness, and fill them with love. And from this again we learn in what the perfection of the Christian life consists — in love and pure holiness of heart, flowing from faith. He recommends love mutually cherished <hi type="italic">towards each other</hi>, and afterwards <hi type="italic">towards all</hi>, for as it is befitting that a commencement should be made with those that are of the <hi type="italic">household of faith</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gal.6.10">Galatians 6:10</reference>) so our love ought to go forth to the whole human race. Farther, as the nearer connection must be cherished, <note n="563"> <div sID="gen128184" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Il faut recognoistre et entretenir</foreign>;” — “We must recognize and maintain.”<div eID="gen128184" type="x-p"/> </note> so we must not overlook those who are farther removed from us, so as to prevent them from holding their proper place.<div eID="gen128183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen128185" type="x-p"/>He would have the Thessalonians abound in love and be filled with it, because in so far as we make progress in acquaintance with God, the love of the brethren must at the same time increase in us, until it take possession of our whole heart, the corrupt love of self being extirpated. He prays that the love of the Thessalonians may be perfected by God, intimating that its increase, no less than its commencement, was from God alone. Hence it is evident how preposterous a part those act who measure our strength by the precepts of the Divine law. <hi type="italic">The end of the law is love</hi>, says Paul, (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Tim.1.5">1 Timothy 1:5</reference>) yet he himself declares that it is a work of God. When, therefore, God marks out our life, <note n="564"> <div sID="gen128186" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Nous prescrit en ses commandemens la regle de viure</foreign>;” — “Prescribes to us in his commandments the rule of life.”<div eID="gen128186" type="x-p"/> </note> he does not look to what we can do, but requires from us what is above our strength, that we may learn to ask from him power to accomplish it. When he says — <hi type="italic">as we also towards you</hi>, he stimulates them by his own example.<div eID="gen128185" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:1Thess.3.12" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen128182" osisID="1Thess.3.12" type="section"/>
entries.35150f1bd3fd8e3037f316d33e4663dd610b399d:
13 That he may confirm your hearts. He employs the term hearts here to mean conscience, or the innermost part of the soul; for he means that a man is acceptable to God only when he brings holiness of heart; that is, not merely external, but also internal. But it is asked, whether by means of holiness we stand at God’s judgment-seat, for if so, to what purpose is remission of sins? Yet Paul’s words seem to imply this — that their consciences might be irreproveable in holiness. I answer, that Paul does not exclude remission of sins, through which it comes that our holiness, which is otherwise mixed up with many pollutions, bears God’s eye, for faith, by which God is pacified towards us, so as to pardon our faults,
“Nous fautes et infirmitez vicieuses;” — “Our faults and culpable infirmities.”
precedes everything else, as the foundation comes before the building. Paul, however, does not teach us what or how great the holiness of believers may be, but desires that it may be increased, until it attain its perfection. On this account he says — at the coming of our Lord, meaning that the completion of those things, which the Lord now begins in us, is delayed till that time.
With all his saints. This clause may be explained in two ways, either as meaning that the Thessalonians, with all saints, may have pure hearts at Christ’s coming, or that Christ will come with all his saints. While I adopt this second meaning, in so far as concerns the construction of the words, I have at the same time no doubt that Paul employed the term saints for the purpose of admonishing us that we are called by Christ for this end—that we may be gathered with all his saints. For this consideration ought to whet our desire for holiness.
CHAPTER 4
1 Thessalonians 4:1-5
1. Furthermore then we beseech you, brethren, and exhort you by the Lord Jesus, that as ye have received of us how ye ought to walk and to please God, so ye would abound more and more.
1. Ergo quod reliquum est, fratres, rogamus vos et obsecramus in Domino Iesu, quemadmodum accepistis a nobis, quomodo oporteat vos ambulare et placere Deo, ut abundetis magis:
2. For ye know what commandments we gave you by the Lord Jesus.
2. Nostis enim quae praecepta dederimus vobis per Dominum Iesum.
3. For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication:
3. Haec enim est voluntas Dei, sanctificatio vestra: ut vos abstineatis ab omni scortatione.
4. That every one of you should know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour;
4. Et sciat unusquisque vestrum suum vas possidere in sanctificatione et honore:
5. Not in the lust of concupiscence, even as the Gentiles which know not God:
5. Non in affectu concupiscentiae, quemadmodum et Gentes, quae non noverunt Deum.

entries.a2a2cd39e1ee722d70f8232c38e23e7cf7465d38:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="3" type="chapter">
               <ns0:head>CHAP. III.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">1 WHerefore when we could no longer for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bear †, we thought it good † to be left at Athens alone:<ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The Apostle proceeds upon the same Argument to confirm his love to them, and care of them, that they might not doubt of it, because of his long absence from them. Therefore he tells them that though he could not come himself, yet he sent <ns0:hi>Timotheus</ns0:hi> to them from <ns0:hi>Athens,</ns0:hi> which we find not menti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />oned in the <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> by <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi>; and his love herein is commended the more, 1. because he sent him out of a strong impulse of affection, he could not forbear any longer, or <ns0:hi>bear,</ns0:hi> it was a hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vy burden to him till he had done it, as the word imports. 2. He was content to be left at <ns0:hi>Athens</ns0:hi> alone by parting with <ns0:hi>Timothy,</ns0:hi> though his company was so desirable and useful to him at that time. And he was well pleased so to do for their sakes, <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> he had a complacence of mind in so doing, so much he preferr'd their good before his own content<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 And sent <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 16.11.</ns0:note> Timotheus our brother and mi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nister of God, and our fellow-labourer in the gospel of Christ, to establish you, and to com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fort you concerning your faith <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">3. By the description he gives of him in the Text. A man dear to him, and as his right hand in the service of the Gospel. And his care of them is commended the more by sending so eminent a person to them. 4. From his end in sending him; which was to establish them, that through the fear of suffering, or any Temptations they might not forsake the Faith they had received; <ns0:hi>and to comfort them concerning their Faith:</ns0:hi> The word sometimes signifies to exhort, and the sence is good if we so read it. But because the Faith they had em<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />braced presented much matter of comfort to them, therefore our Translation well renders the word.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Eph. 3.13.</ns0:note> That no man should be moved <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>shaken.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> by these afflictions <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The word here used by the Apostle answers another word used 2 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 2.2. which alludes to the waves of the Sea shaken by the winds. Fears, and doubts, or haesitations of mind do move and shake it, which the Apostle sent <ns0:hi>Timothy</ns0:hi> to prevent, or remove.</ns0:note>, for your selves know that we are appointed thereunto <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">And besides he addeth an argument of his own to confirm them when he tells them, <ns0:hi>ye know that we are appointed thereunto</ns0:hi>; The word is used <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 2.34. 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 1.9. But he means we suffer afflictions according to the purpose and intention of God. They come not by chance, or meerly from mens wrath and en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mity, but from the appointment of God. And whether the Apostle speaks only of his own sufferings, and other Ministers of the Gospel, or of all Saints in general, as <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 14.22. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.17, 30. 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 3.12. is uncertain, we may well understand it of both; so that he would not have these <ns0:hi>Thessalonians</ns0:hi> think it strange, as if some strange thing happened to them, 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 4.12. whereby to be shaken in their minds.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>called, set, appointed, desti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ned.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.<ns0:note place="bottom">The Apostle had mentioned before his great afflictions, and they knew well what he himself had suffered both at <ns0:hi>Thessalonica</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Berea, Acts</ns0:hi> 16. and therefore might fear they might here<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />upon be shaken in their Faith. And <ns0:hi>Timothy</ns0:hi> therefore was sent to comfort and establish them: God could do this without him, but the Ministry is his ordinance he works by. And when he saith that <ns0:hi>no man should be moved</ns0:hi>; it shews what is a Christi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ans Duty to be unmoved by sufferings for the Gospel.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 For verily, when we were with you we told you before that we should suffer tribulation <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">The Apostle having said that they knew they were ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pointed to sufferings, tells them here they knew it, because he had told them of it. <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> by some extraordinary instinct or Revelation often foresaw his sufferings, and God more general<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly told him of them at his first Conversion, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 9.16. And he told them of them that they might reckon upon sufferings. A faithful Minister will not only tell the people of the Crown, but of the Cross of Christ.</ns0:note>, even as it came to pass, and ye know <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">And what he foretold of his sufferings, he tells them came to pass, whereby they might be strengthened further in their Faith about the Gospel he had preached to them, and not be offended at his sufferings, being foretold to them, as well as appointed of God.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 For this cause when I could no longer for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bear, I sent to know your faith, lest by some means the tempter had tempted you <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">The Apostle here gives a further account of the reason why he sent <ns0:hi>Timotheus</ns0:hi> to them, which was to know their Faith, whether it continued stedfast under all their sufferings and temptations. He feared Satan whom he calls the Tempter, might have some way or other tempted them, either by false Tea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />chers to seduce them, or by sufferings to affright them. He was more concerned about the inward State of their Souls, than their outward Condition; and commonly temptations go along with persecutions:</ns0:note>, and our labour <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Phil. 2.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> be in vain <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">And the Apostle having bestowed great labour upon them, feared, lest it might be in vain, that the Tempter had prevailed. Satans first work is to keep men from believing, his next is to destroy their Faith; young Converts are com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />monly most assaulted. <ns0:hi>Pauls</ns0:hi> heart was therefore very solicitous for them, so that (as he said before) he could not any longer forbear sending to know how it was with them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 But now, when Timotheus came from you to us, and brought us good tydings of your faith <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">We had before an account of <ns0:hi>Timothies</ns0:hi> sending, now of his return, wherein we have the message he brought, and the effect thereof upon the Apostle. The message may be consi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dered, 1. As to its new-coming, <ns0:hi>But now when Timotheus came,</ns0:hi> &c. so that this Epistle seems to be writ presently upon his re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />turn. 2. As to the good account it brought of them, <ns0:hi>It brought good tydings</ns0:hi>; (the same word is here used that expresseth in the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> the glad tydings of the Gospel) of their Faith, that it continued still stedfast.</ns0:note> and charity <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>love.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="k" place="margin">And of their Charity or Love, that they had Love joyned with their Faith, and their Faith working by Love, which shewed it was living, and of a right kind.</ns0:note>, and that ye have good remembrance of us alwaies <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">They forgot him not, though absent some length of time from them; and it was a good remembrance joyned with Love and Esteem of his Person, and of his Ministry amongst them; and it was <ns0:hi>alwaies,</ns0:hi> which implies the constancy of it.</ns0:note>, desiring greatly to see us <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">And not satisfied with this good remembrance of him being absent, they greatly desired his presence to see him and his fellow-labourers.</ns0:note>, as we also <ns0:hi>to see</ns0:hi> you <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">And to answer their Love on his part, he addeth, <ns0:hi>as we also to see you.</ns0:hi> By all which he seeks to satisfie them of his continued care and remembrance of them, which was the effect of this message.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 Therefore, brethren, we were comforted over you <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>is y<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, in all our affliction, and distress by your faith <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">He was comforted by this Faith of theirs in all his own affliction, and distress. The faithfulness and constancy of a people is the great comfort of their Teachers. <ns0:hi>I have no grea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter joy than to see my Children walking in the truth,</ns0:hi> 2 Joh. 3, 4.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 For now we live, if ye stand fast in the Lord <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">The comfort of their Faith was so great that it would be as Life to him, if they stood fast in it; which he calls a <ns0:hi>standing fast in the Lord.</ns0:hi> Life is not only the Union of Soul and Body, Comfort is the Life of the Soul, especially that which springs from divine causes. And on the contrary the apostacy and de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />generacy of a people doth kill the hearts of their faithful Teachers.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 For what thanks can we render to God again for you, for all the joy wherewith we joy for your sakes <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">This is another effect of the message <ns0:hi>Timothy</ns0:hi> brought, it caused in the Apostle great Thanksgivings to God. First he re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />joyced in their Faith, and then gives thanks to God for that joy. The matter of his rejoycing was their Faith, but the author and upholder of this Faith was God; and in giving thanks to God for his joy he gives thanks also to God for their faith from whence it sprang. The joy that Ministers have in their peoples Faith should break forth into Thanksgivings. And the Apostles thanks to God was beyond what he could return or express, as appears by the form of his speech, <ns0:hi>For what thanks can we render,</ns0:hi> &c. as <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 116.12. <ns0:hi>What shall I return unto the Lord,</ns0:hi> said <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note> before our God <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">And his rejoycing before God implyes <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>o<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ly the nature of it, it was divine and spiritual, and his respect to God therein, as <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> danced <ns0:hi>before the Lord</ns0:hi> with all his might, 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 6.14. <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> With a respect to Gods goodness then de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clared. Or the Apostle may mean his joy was inward before God, rather then before men.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:517" />Night and day <ns0:note place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">

                     </ns0:gap> 1.10, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                  </ns0:note> praying exceedingly <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">We have here the last effect of <ns0:hi>Timotheus</ns0:hi> message, upon the Apostle, it put him upon Prayer for these <ns0:hi>Thessalonians,</ns0:hi> exprest by the assiduity of it, <ns0:hi>night and day,</ns0:hi> &c. that is in a constant course; as we noted before <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 2.9. And by the fervency of it, <ns0:hi>exceedingly,</ns0:hi> or excessively. The greek word cannot well be Englished, yet often used by the Apostle when he would ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />press any thing with an emphasis, as <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 3.20. and in this Epistle, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 5.13.</ns0:note> that we might see your face, and might perfect that which is lacking in your faith <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">And by the matter of it; <ns0:hi>That he might see their face, and perfect that which was lacking in their Faith.</ns0:hi> Though his Epistles might avail towards it, yet his personal presence would do more. There is a peculiar blessing attends oral Preaching, more then reading. The like Prayer he made, with respect to the Romans, and upon the same account also <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.10, 11. Though the Apostle had before commended their Faith, yea there was something lacking in it. No Faith is made perfect at first; yea the best Faith may have some de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fects. And the word is used else where to signifie something that is wanting, or left behind, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 16.17. and <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 1.24. and their Faith might be defective as to the matter of it, some mysteries of Faith they might not yet understand, as the Disci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ples did not, till after Christs Ascension, and some of the <ns0:hi>Corin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thians a while doubted</ns0:hi> the Doctrine of the Resurrection, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 15.12. &c. 2. As to the clearness of it with respect to the Truths they did already know and believe. 3. As to the lively operations and fruits of it. The former defects are removed by Doctrine, the last by Exhortation, and Comfort, and the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle desired to see their face on the account of both: And to perfect a thing is to make it compleat both as to parts and de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />grees. The word here used we find it oft in the New Testament, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 13.11. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 6.1. &c. and variously rendred in the several translations, but yet much to the same sense; the Apostle be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing so suddenly driven from them, he left them as an house half built; but his affection to them was so great, that he longed to return to them for the perfecting of their Faith, though he had met but a while before with such great perils at <ns0:hi>Thessalonica.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 Now God himself, and our Father <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Here his Prayer is exprest, the persons to whom he prayes is God himself, personally considered as God the Father, and relatively, when he stiles him <ns0:hi>our Father</ns0:hi>; so ought beleivers to address themselves to God not absolutely, but as to their Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther. So Christ taught his Disciples to pray, <ns0:hi>Our Father</ns0:hi>; and so the Spirit of Adoption doth prompt the Saints to pray: we come to God with greater freedom and confidence when we can come to him as a Father.</ns0:note>, and our Lord Jesus Christ <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">And he prayes also to Christ, whom he stiles <ns0:hi>our Lord Iesus Christ.</ns0:hi> Whence we may have an argument that Christ is God, else he could not be the object of di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vine Worship, not that we are to present our Prayers distinctly to the Son without considering his Union with the Father, nor to the father distinctly from the Son, but to the Father in and by the Lord Jesus Christ. For so only we can consider him as our Father in Prayer. And he speaks of Christ also in his relation to his people, <ns0:hi>our Lord Iesus Christ,</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>

                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> direct our way unto you <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">And the thing he Prays for, is, that <ns0:hi>God would direct his way unto them,</ns0:hi> that the hindran<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ces of Satan whatsoever they were might be removed, and the Providence of God open him a way to come to them: the word <ns0:hi>direct</ns0:hi> signifies in the Greek to make straight, and 2 <ns0:hi>Thess:</ns0:hi> 3.5. is applyed to the heart. <ns0:hi>The Lord direct your hearts,</ns0:hi> &c. which is setting the heart straight towards God, answering to the Hebrew word <ns0:hi>Iashar,</ns0:hi> which signifies to be upright, and is often used in the Old Testament. The French read it, address our way. And hence we learn our Duty by the Apostles practise to pray to have our way in all cases directed by God.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 And the Lord make you to increase and abound <ns0:note place="margin">

                     </ns0:gap> 1.15.</ns0:note> in love one towards another <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">This is another thing he praies for, the former respected himself, this respected them. He desired to come to them to perfect that which was lacking in their Faith, and he prays now for the abounding and increase of their Love, not only to love one another, but to encrease and abound in it. To encrease the habits and abound in the fruits of love. They were under sore persecutions, and their Love to one another was more necessary at such a time.</ns0:note>, and towards all men <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">And not only to one ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, but to extend their love towards all men. Either all men in general; for love is a general duty we owe to all men, <ns0:hi>Owe nothing to any one but to love one another, Rom.</ns0:hi> 13.8. And therefore all our duty to men is comprehended under it. And the Apostle requires this love to be added to brotherly kind<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness, 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 1.7. yea love is required to Enemies, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 5.44. though not as Enemies yet as Men, or more particularly, Beleivers: as sometimes <ns0:hi>all men</ns0:hi> is taken under that restriction, <ns0:hi>Tit.</ns0:hi> 2.11.</ns0:note>, even as we <ns0:hi>do</ns0:hi> towards you <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">And he setteth before them his own love to <ns0:hi>them,</ns0:hi> both as a pattern and motive hereunto, Though the love of Christ is especially to be looked at, and is proposed often by the Apostle <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> as the great argument of love to men, yet he mentions his own love to them here to shew the constancy of his affection to them though absent from them, and to shew that he perswaded no duty to them but what he practised him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self.</ns0:note>,<ns0:note n="†" place="margin">These two words denote an encreasing and overflowing abundance.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 To the end he may <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 1.8. Phil. 1.10. chap. 5.23. 2 Thess<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 2.17.</ns0:note> stablish your hearts unblameable in holiness before God even our Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">These words some referr only to the verse immediately pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceding; by encreasing and abounding in love, their hearts would be establisht unblameable in holiness. Which is true, for that holiness is justly to be suspected, at least is to be blam<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed which is without love to men. And love it self is a great part of holiness, and who will blame holiness when it shines forth in love, yea it will be unblamable before God and Men. And when God doth cause a people to encrease in Love, he doth hereby establish them in Holiness that is unblameable; where love is wanting the heart is not established. The hypocrite will fall off in an hour of Temptation, because he wants love; and though he may for a while make a fair shew before men, yet he is not unblameable before God who searcheth the heart: neither will he be found so at the appearance of Jesus Christ; which the Apostle prayes for here with respect to these <ns0:hi>Thessa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lonians,</ns0:hi> that they might be establisht in holiness until the coming of Christ; or that they might be found unblameable in holiness at his coming. Whereby the Apostle signifies there is yet ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther coming of Christ, then there will a strict trial pass upon men, and therefore the Saints should labour to be then found unblameable, or without spot and blemish, as 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 3.14.</ns0:note> with all his saints <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Whereof he gives a particular account in the next chapter, others carry this verse as referring also to the 11th. verse where he desired to see their face to perfect their Faith, that both by their Faith and Love, they might be establisht unblameable in holiness.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
